title: Wading through water
caption: The ram-pressure stripped tail of the galaxy D100, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope and the Subaru Telescope
celestial: D100, LEDA 44716, Mrk 60 · constellation Coma Berenices · about 350 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A plume of gas trails away from the spiral galaxy nicknamed D100. The image shows only part of the tail, which extends well beyond the frame to the left. It combines data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys with data from the Subaru Telescope in Hawaii.

D100 belongs to the huge Coma cluster, and its tail is the product of ram-pressure stripping. The space between a cluster's galaxies is far from empty. It holds very hot gas and plasma, known as the intracluster medium, that drags at galaxies as they travel through it, much like the resistance you feel wading through deep water. This pressure has pulled gas out of D100 and drawn it into a long plume.
The effect can be powerful enough to pull galaxies to pieces, leaving some with bizarre shapes. Crowded clusters such as Coma, home to thousands of galaxies, are ideal places to study it.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (1.82 x 1.37 arcminutes) and distance (350 million light years), the frame spans roughly 185,000 × 139,000 light-years. Its light set out about 350 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This combines visible-light Hubble data from the Advanced Camera for Surveys, at 475 nm and 814 nm, with data from the Subaru Telescope. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The combined Hubble and Subaru exposures collect far more light than an eye can.

behind.people: See full credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, Cramer et al.
behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Ram-pressure stripping matters beyond its looks. By removing gas, it can have a profound effect on how galaxies change and on whether they go on forming new generations of stars.
alt: A spiral galaxy with a long plume of gas streaming away from it to one side.
